title: Artefacts Associated With Cryogenic Vacuum Distillation Do Not Compromise Plant Source Water Extraction From Soil and Xylem for Isotope Analysis
content:
ABSTRACT

Understanding the oxygen and hydrogen isotopic composition (δ18O and δ2H values, respectively) of plant source water is fundamental for tracing water uptake in ecohydrological studies. However, discrepancies between cryogenic vacuum distillation (CVD)-extracted soil and xylem water and known plant source water δ18O and δ2H values continue to raise concerns about the accuracy of this approach, especially for δ2H. We conducted two irrigation experiments on juvenile temperate trees to evaluate the accuracy by which CVD soil and xylem water characterize the δ18O and δ2H values of plant source water. To do this, we compared the δ18O and δ2H of irrigation and mildly vacuum-extracted (MVE) sap water, which has previously been shown to characterize plant source water δ18O and δ2H values with high accuracy, with those of CVD-extracted water from soil, xylem and phloem δ18O and δ2H values. In both experiments, irrigation water and MVE sap δ18O and δ2H values were similar to each other. We yet observed a small and consistent offset between δ18O and δ2H values of irrigation water and CVD-extracted soil water δ18O and δ2H values. These offsets indicate that CVD soil water captures a mixture of two isotopically distinct soil water pools: a mobile, plant-available pool and an immobile, plant-unavailable pool. Primarily δ2H values of CVD-extracted xylem water differed from both CVD-extracted water from MVE sap and phloem, while δ18O differences were minimal. This suggests that artefacts associated with CVD, rather than stem evaporation or phloem–xylem exchange, were the primary source of the observed δ2H offsets. In summary, our findings demonstrate that CVD is a valid extraction method for accurate plant source water δ18O values while δ2H values are associated with artefacts that require correction.
